sandhi.note: -āḥ before a voiced consonant loses its visarga.
Final t becomes d before the voiced r. The final m of रुधिरम् becomes anusvāra before m (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).

morph.note: Present of √शी ‘to lie’: the root takes guṇa throughout (शे-), and the 3rd plural inserts r before the ending (शे-र-ते). The present here is the narrative (historic) present: ‘they lie’ amid perfects.
Perfect of √वम् in the form without reduplication, with e in the root (वेमुः, like पेचुः from √पच्); grammarians allow it for √वम् beside the reduplicated ववमुः.
kta from the causative stem पोथय- of √पुथ् (the causative suffix drops before -इत): ‘made to be crushed’, i.e. pounded flat.

mantras.anvaya: (अपरे) गदया निपातेन विपोथिताः भुवि शेरते। केचित् च मुसलेन भृशं हताः रुधिरं वेमुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first sentence has its subject, अपरे, at the end of 2.57. Each clause: participle(s) + instrumental of means + finite verb.
mantras.lit: (others,) crushed by the blow, by the mace, lie on the ground. And some, struck hard by the club, vomited blood.
mantras.tr: others lie on the ground, crushed by the blows of her mace; and some, struck hard by her club, spewed blood.
mantras.tr_note: निपातेन गदया, two instrumentals side by side (‘by the blow, with the mace’), are rendered as one phrase.

comm.t: Two more weapons, two more deaths: the mace crushes, the musala (club) makes the asuras spew blood. The verse moves into the present (शेरते ‘they lie’), as if the narrator were looking at the field.

The mace (गदा) is among the weapons held by Mahālakṣmī in the Gita Press dhyāna for this carita (… गदेषुकुलिशं …); that the middle carita is presided over by Mahālakṣmī is the liturgical tradition of the pāṭha, not a statement of the Purāṇa.

samasa.literal: those from whom (every) gap has gone
samasa.sense: so densely covered with arrows that no space was left on their bodies
by her storm of arrows (from the bow and quiver Vāyu gave her, 2.21)

morph.note: kta of √भिद् with -न instead of -त (d + n → nn): भिन्न ‘split, pierced’.
kta of √पत् with the connecting vowel i (पतित). Intransitive, so active in sense: ‘fallen’.

mantras.anvaya: केचित् वक्षसि शूलेन भिन्नाः भूमौ निपतिताः। केचित् रणाजिरे शरौघेण निरन्तराः कृताः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two parallel sentences, each with केचित् and a participle for the verb; the second has a predicate adjective (निरन्तराः) with कृताः.
mantras.lit: Some fell on the ground, pierced in the chest by the spear. Some were made gapless by a flood of arrows on the battlefield.
mantras.tr: Some, pierced through the chest by her spear, fell to the ground; some, on the field of battle, were riddled through and through by her storm of arrows.

comm.t: The catalogue continues: the śūla pierces the chest, the arrows leave no space unwounded. निरन्तर, ‘without interval’, pictures bodies covered with arrows from end to end.

samasa.type: upapada tatpuruṣa (second member the agent noun अनुकारिन्, अनु + √कृ + णिनि)
samasa.sense: falling as a hawk drops — said of the dying asuras
samasa.alt: अनुकारिणः is also the accusative plural, so it can agree with प्राणान्: ‘they released their breaths, which (flew off) like hawks’. Both constructions are grammatical; this edition takes it with the subject, the nearer reading of an epithet in -इन्, and records the other.

samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (the second member the agent noun अर्दन ‘tormenting’, from √अर्द्)
samasa.sense: the asuras, oppressors of the gods (त्रिदश ‘the Thirty’ is a standard name for the gods, from the round number of the thirty-three)

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (feminine ग्रीवा shortened to -ग्रीव at the end of a bahuvrīhi qualifying a masculine)

morph.note: The indefinite pronoun is the interrogative किम् declined + the particle चित्: genitive plural केषाम् + चित् ‘of some’. The final m is written as anusvāra before c inside this one word.
Perfect 3rd plural of √मुच् (weak stem मुमुच्), beside मुमोच (3rd sg., 2.51) and मुमुचे (ātmanepada, 2.52).

mantras.anvaya: श्येनानुकारिणः त्रिदशार्दनाः प्राणान् मुमुचुः। केषांचित् बाहवः छिन्नाः, तथा अपरे छिन्नग्रीवाः (अभवन्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line is a complete sentence (subject at the end). The second gives two short clauses with the verb ‘to be’ understood.
mantras.lit: The tormentors of the gods, imitating hawks, released their life-breaths. Of some the arms were cut off; likewise others had their necks cut.
mantras.tr: Like hawks dropping from the sky, the tormentors of the gods gave up their lives. Some had their arms hewn off, and others their heads struck from their necks.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Dropping from the sky’ interprets श्येनानुकारिणः ‘imitating hawks’, which the Sanskrit leaves unexplained; see Samāsa for the other construction.

comm.t: The asuras are called त्रिदशार्दनाः, ‘tormentors of the Thirty’, at the moment they die: the epithet recalls why the battle is fought (2.6–8). The second line goes on cataloguing wounds — arms, necks.

flags.uncertain: The point of comparison in श्येनानुकारिणः is not stated: it may describe the asuras (falling as hawks drop) or, as an accusative, their departing breaths (flying off like hawks). Both constructions are recorded; the choice is interpretive.

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (feminine जङ्घा shortened to -जङ्घ at the end of a bahuvrīhi qualifying a masculine)
samasa.sense: hamstrung, their legs cut from under them

morph.note: Perfect 3rd plural of √पत् without reduplication: the root vowel becomes e (पेत्-), as regularly in roots of the shape C-a-C with an unchanged initial consonant (compare वेमुः, 2.58).
kta from the causative दारय- of √दॄ ‘to burst, tear’: ‘torn open’. मध्ये ‘in the middle’ says where: cut through at the waist.

mantras.anvaya: अन्येषां शिरांसि पेतुः। अन्ये मध्ये विदारिताः। अपरे तु महासुराः विच्छिन्नजङ्घाः उर्व्यां पेतुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three clauses, each with its own subject: heads fell; others were split; still others fell hamstrung.
mantras.lit: The heads of others fell; others were torn apart in the middle; and other great asuras, their legs cut off, fell on the earth.
mantras.tr: Others’ heads fell; others were split through the middle; and still other great asuras, their legs hewn away, fell to the earth.

comm.t: The anatomy of the slaughter continues — heads, waists, legs. The repetition of पेतुः ‘fell’ frames the verse.
A modern reading: the unflinching detail of these verses is not cruelty for its own sake. The text wants the defeat of what oppresses the gods to be total and visible, limb by limb.

samasa.vigraha: एकः बाहुः एकम् अक्षि एकः चरणः च येषां ते; बाह्वक्षिचरणाः = बाहुः च अक्षि च चरणः च
samasa.literal: those whose arm, eye and foot are (each) one
samasa.sense: split lengthwise, so that each half has a single arm, eye and foot

morph.note: Locative absolute (sati saptamī): छिन्ने शिरसि ‘the head having been cut off’, with अपि ‘even when …’. The participle agrees with शिरसि in neuter locative singular.
kta of उद् + √स्था: स्था weakens to स्थि (स्थित), and the s is lost after the prefix उद् (उद् + स्थित → उत्थित).

mantras.anvaya: केचित् देव्या द्विधा कृताः एकबाह्वक्षिचरणाः (अभवन्)। अन्ये च शिरसि छिन्ने अपि पतिताः पुनः उत्थिताः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first sentence explains the compound: cut in two, they were left with one arm, eye and foot. The second sentence continues into 2.63, where the risen trunks fight.
mantras.lit: Some, cut in two by the Devī, (were left) with one arm, one eye, one foot. And others, even when the head was cut off, having fallen rose up again.
mantras.tr: Some the Goddess cleft in two, leaving each half one arm, one eye, one foot. And others, though their heads were struck off, fell and rose again —

comm.t: The battle turns grotesque: asuras split lengthwise, and headless bodies that fall and stand up again. The next two verses describe these headless trunks (कबन्ध) fighting on.
Headless trunks (कबन्ध) rising and fighting on are a familiar image in epic battle descriptions. Here it marks the asuras’ ferocity: they resist even past death, and it is still not enough.
